steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our WeatherDepth paper on self-supervised depth estimation under adverse weather using curriculum contrastive learning. Explain the problem and the shortcomings of existing approaches, describe the curricula, the contrastive designs, the scheduler and the dataset, and end with experiments and contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Depth estimation, self-supervision, and the adverse weather problem; limits of recent work
- WeatherDepth: three simple-to-complex curricula
- Contrastive learning against forgetting
- Adaptive curriculum scheduler and WeatherKITTI
- Evaluation and contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Problem
  - depth estimation bridges 2D images and 3D scenes; applications: 3D reconstruction (cite), autonomous driving
  - GT-depth from LiDARs etc. costly -> self-supervised: photometric consistency between depth-based reconstructed and target images
  - adverse weather: sharp precision drop; particles break consistency assumption; illumination variation -> domain gap
  - recent work: restore clear scenes (cite), features consistent with sunny (cite x2), distillation from clear scenes (cite x2)
  - ignore varying degrees/categories of weather; augmentation unrealistic (Fig. 2)
- WeatherDepth curricula
  - self-supervised robust depth model via curriculum contrastive learning
  - clear -> relatively adverse -> adverse; three simple-to-complex curricula
  - 1: base model on sunny data, clear structures, photometric consistency; better-generalizable local optima for pre-training (cite)
  - 2: relative adverse: light effects, ground snow and water; share regions with clear domain; depth cues despite missing textures/contrasts
  - 3: adverse with weather particles (e.g. raindrops); complex noise, violations of self-supervised assumptions
- Contrastive designs
  - pre-defined curriculum alone -> catastrophic forgetting (cite), big inter-domain difference per stage
  - light-weight contrastive learning in each curriculum (Fig. 3)
  - mode 1: two clear images with different traditional enhancements (cite); robust to depth-irrelevant info
  - then 3 modes: sunny vs random rainy/snowy/foggy; avoids biasing to new weather
  - last: 3 adverse vs 3 relative adverse = 9 modes; cross-weather robustness, less forgetting
  - 1 -> 3 -> 9: second curriculum by contrastive difficulty; easier convergence
- Scheduler + data
  - adaptive curriculum scheduler auto-switches curricula; less manual intervention, smoother transitions
  - GAN + PBR (cite) -> WeatherKITTI, diverse categories and magnitudes
  - more realistic than existing augmented data (cite x3), Fig. 2
- Evaluation + contributions
  - plugged into PlaneDepth, WaveletMonodepth, MonoViT
  - beats SoTA on synthetic and real weather datasets
  - first to apply curriculum contrastive learning to depth estimation
  - contributions: strategy (extendable to other simple-to-complex tasks); scheduler + WeatherKITTI; extensive experiments

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Depth estimation connects 2D images with 3D scenes and it has many potential applications, for example 3D reconstruction and autonomous driving. In recent years, collecting GT-depth from LiDARs and other sensors has high costs, so researchers have turned to self-supervised solutions that use the photometric consistency between the images reconstructed from depth and the target images. But under adverse weather conditions the depth precision drops sharply, since weather particles break the consistency assumption and illumination variations create an inevitable domain gap. Recent works tried to reduce this performance degradation by restoring clear weather scenes, extracting features that are consistent with sunny conditions, knowledge distillation from clear scenes, and so on. But these solutions do not consider that weather comes in different degrees and categories, and their data augmentation does not reflect real situations well (Fig. 2), and this limits what the estimation algorithm can do under weather conditions.

In this paper we propose a self-supervised robust depth estimation model, called WeatherDepth, that addresses these issues with curriculum contrastive learning. First, we simulate the progression from clear to relatively adverse and then to adverse weather scenes, and build three curricula from simple to complex with adverse weather to different degrees. We first train a base model on sunny data, which has clear structures, so that photometric consistency holds. This lets the model get local optima that generalize better for pre-training on more complex scenarios. Then we optimize the model on relative adverse weather images with light effects, ground snow and water. These share some common regions with the clear domain and encourage the model to gradually learn the depth cues despite missing textures and contrasts. Finally we train the model on adverse data where weather particles (e.g., raindrops) are added, which further improves its ability to handle complex noise patterns and violations of the self-supervised assumptions.

- Contrastive designs against forgetting
  - curriculum alone -> catastrophic forgetting; light-weight contrastive learning in each curriculum (Fig. 3)
  - 1 mode: two clear images, different traditional enhancements
  - 3 modes: sunny vs random rainy/snowy/foggy
  - 9 modes: 3 adverse vs 3 relative adverse
  - 1 -> 3 -> 9 = curriculum by contrastive difficulty; easier convergence
- Adaptive curriculum scheduler; WeatherKITTI via GAN + PBR; more realistic than existing augmented data (Fig. 2)
- Evaluation: PlaneDepth, WaveletMonodepth, MonoViT; beats SoTA on synthetic and real; first curriculum contrastive learning for depth
- Contributions: strategy; scheduler + WeatherKITTI; extensive experiments

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Depth estimation connects 2D images with 3D scenes and it has many potential applications, for example 3D reconstruction and autonomous driving. In recent years, collecting GT-depth from LiDARs and other sensors has high costs, so researchers have turned to self-supervised solutions that use the photometric consistency between the images reconstructed from depth and the target images. But under adverse weather conditions the depth precision drops sharply, since weather particles break the consistency assumption and illumination variations create an inevitable domain gap. Recent works tried to reduce this performance degradation by restoring clear weather scenes, extracting features that are consistent with sunny conditions, knowledge distillation from clear scenes, and so on. But these solutions do not consider that weather comes in different degrees and categories, and their data augmentation does not reflect real situations well (Fig. 2), and this limits what the estimation algorithm can do under weather conditions.

In this paper we propose a self-supervised robust depth estimation model, called WeatherDepth, that addresses these issues with curriculum contrastive learning. First, we simulate the progression from clear to relatively adverse and then to adverse weather scenes, and build three curricula from simple to complex with adverse weather to different degrees. We first train a base model on sunny data, which has clear structures, so that photometric consistency holds. This lets the model get local optima that generalize better for pre-training on more complex scenarios. Then we optimize the model on relative adverse weather images with light effects, ground snow and water. These share some common regions with the clear domain and encourage the model to gradually learn the depth cues despite missing textures and contrasts. Finally we train the model on adverse data where weather particles (e.g., raindrops) are added, which further improves its ability to handle complex noise patterns and violations of the self-supervised assumptions.

Second, a pre-defined curriculum learning alone may cause catastrophic forgetting because the domains are very different in each stage. So we put light-weight contrastive learning designs into the different curricula. As shown in Fig. 3, we first set up one contrastive mode between two clear images that have different traditional enhancements. This makes the network more robust to this information that is irrelevant to depth and prepares it for the weather variation in the later courses. Then we build three harder contrastive modes between the sunny scene and randomly selected rainy/snowy/foggy weather scenes. This stops the network from only focusing on resisting weather changes and from completely biasing its domain to the new weather. In the last curriculum we contrast three adverse weather against three relative adverse weather, which gives nine contrastive modes, to improve cross-weather robustness and reduce forgetting. The contrastive modes get harder and harder (from 1 to 3 to 9), so they form another curriculum learning process based on contrastive difficulty, and this helps the training converge easily.

We also propose an adaptive curriculum scheduler that switches curricula automatically. It needs less manual intervention and the transitions between courses are smoother. To train the model we want and to make the domain gap to real weather conditions smaller, we combine GAN and PBR techniques and build the WeatherKITTI dataset, which has diverse categories and magnitudes of weather. Its weather scenes are more realistic than existing augmented weather data, as shown in Fig. 2.

Finally, to evaluate how effective it is, we put the proposed curriculum contrastive learning scheme into three popular depth estimation baselines (PlaneDepth, WaveletMonodepth, and MonoViT). The experiments show that the WeatherDepth models are better than the existing SoTA solutions on both synthetic and real weather datasets. As far as we know, this is the first work that applies curriculum contrastive learning to depth estimation. The main contributions are:

- • We propose a curriculum contrastive learning strategy with robust weather adaption, so that the model adapts to adverse weather without forgetting knowledge. It can be used with various SoTA depth estimation schemes and could be extended to other simple-to-complex prediction tasks.

- • We design an adaptive curriculum scheduler that switches the course automatically by searching for the best timing, which reduces manual intervention and adapts better to different models. We also built the WeatherKITTI dataset to make the domain gap to real weather situations smaller.

- • We do extensive experiments that show our curriculum contrastive learning scheme works on various architectures and performs better than the existing SoTA solutions.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Depth estimation builds a bridge between 2D images and 3D scenes and has numerous potential applications such as 3D reconstruction [1] and autonomous driving. In recent years, due to the high costs of collecting GT-depth from LiDARs and other sensors, researchers have turned to self-supervised solutions that exploit the photometric consistency between depth-based reconstructed images and the target images. However, depth precision drops sharply under adverse weather conditions, because weather particles spoil the consistency assumption and illumination variations produce an inevitable domain gap. Recent works have tried to mitigate this degradation by restoring clear weather scenes [2], extracting features consistent with sunny conditions [3,4], knowledge distillation from clear scenes [5,6], etc. However, these solutions do not account for the fact that weather comes in varying degrees and categories, and their data augmentation does not reflect real situations well (Fig. 2), which limits the potential of the estimation algorithm under weather conditions.

In this paper, we propose a self-supervised robust depth estimation model (named WeatherDepth) that addresses the above issues through curriculum contrastive learning. On the one hand, we simulate the progression from clear to relatively adverse and then adverse weather scenes, building three simple-to-complex curricula with adverse weather to different degrees. Concretely, we first train a base model on sunny data with clear structures to satisfy photometric consistency. This allows the model to obtain better-generalizable local optima for pre-training on more complex scenarios [7]. Then we optimize the model on relative adverse weather images with light effects, ground snow and water, which share some common regions with the clear domain and encourage the model to gradually grasp depth cues despite missing textures and contrasts. Finally, we train the model on adverse data with added weather particles (e.g., raindrops), further boosting its capability to handle complex noise patterns and violations of the self-supervised assumptions.

On the other hand, pre-defined curriculum learning alone may lead to catastrophic forgetting [9] due to the substantial inter-domain difference in each stage. To this end, we embed light-weight contrastive learning designs in the different curricula. As shown in Fig. 3, we first establish one contrastive mode between two clear images with different traditional enhancements [10]. This forces the network to become more robust to this depth-irrelevant information and prepares it for the weather variation in later courses. Then, we build three more challenging contrastive modes between the sunny scene and randomly selected rainy/snowy/foggy weather scenes, which prevents the network from focusing solely on resisting weather changes and completely biasing its domain to the new weather. In the last curriculum, we contrast three adverse weather against three relative adverse weather, constructing nine contrastive modes to improve cross-weather robustness and relieve the problem of forgetting. These increasingly challenging contrastive modes (from 1 to 3 to 9) form another curriculum learning process based on contrastive difficulty, which helps the training converge easily.

Moreover, we propose an adaptive curriculum scheduler to switch curricula automatically, which reduces manual intervention and produces smoother course transitions. To train the expected model and shrink the domain gap to real weather conditions, we combine GAN and PBR techniques [11] to build the WeatherKITTI dataset with diverse categories and magnitudes of weather. Compared with existing augmented weather data [5,8,2], it renders more realistic weather scenes, as shown in Fig. 2.

Finally, we incorporate the proposed curriculum contrastive learning scheme into three popular depth estimation baselines (PlaneDepth, WaveletMonodepth, and MonoViT) to evaluate its effectiveness. Experimental results show that the proposed WeatherDepth models outperform the existing SoTA solutions on both synthetic and real weather datasets. To our knowledge, this is the first work to apply curriculum contrastive learning to depth estimation. The main contributions are summarized as follows:

- • To adapt to adverse weather without forgetting knowledge, we propose a curriculum contrastive learning strategy with robust weather adaption. It can be applied to various SoTA depth estimation schemes and could be extended to other simple-to-complex prediction tasks.

- • To reduce manual intervention and better adapt to different models, we design an adaptive curriculum scheduler that automatically switches the course by searching for the best timing. Besides, we built the WeatherKITTI dataset to narrow the domain gap to real weather situations.

- • We conduct extensive experiments to prove the universality of our curriculum contrastive learning scheme across architectures and its superior performance over the existing SoTA solutions.
